transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess what finally got me to come in is… I’ve been organizing my whole life around avoiding anything that reminds me of that old job. It sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but I’ll drive out of my way so I don’t pass certain office buildings, and if there’s a networking event or some work-related thing near a job site, I just won’t go. I make up reasons—traffic, family stuff, not feeling well—whatever sounds believable.

And it’s not just places. If someone starts talking about security procedures, or “workplace safety,” or anything that even kind of points back to that environment, I tense up and find a way to leave. The worst is if people ask about the day it happened. I can feel myself shutting down, and before I know it I’m saying I need to take a call or I have to get something from my car, and then I’m gone.

I’ve always been someone who handles things—I managed people, handled operations, kept things moving—but this… I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job, and it’s gotten hard to pretend it’s just being busy or practical.
Can you tell me a bit more about what happened at that job or around that time that feels so important to avoid?

It was a confrontation at the job. I can talk around it better than I can talk straight through it, if that makes sense. I remember the buildup, and I remember the fallout almost too clearly — every little thing they said I should have done differently afterward, every mistake they pinned on me, every conversation where I felt like I was being judged or blamed.

But the actual confrontation… there’s this part that’s just missing.

I remember seeing the gun. That part is very clear, like my brain took a picture of it. And then right after that, it’s like someone cut a section out of the film. I’ve tried to piece it together so many times — what was said, who moved first, how long it lasted, what I did — and I can’t. I get bits around the edges, but that chunk itself is just blank.

And that bothers me because I’m not usually like that. I’m the person who remembers details, who keeps track of what happened and who said what. But with that moment, no matter how hard I try, it just isn’t there. I can tell you the things they blamed me for afterward in order, practically word for word, but right after I saw that gun, my mind just… goes empty.
Since that time, have you found yourself feeling constantly on edge, anxious, or overwhelmed when you think about what happened or when something reminds you of it?

Yes. I mean, I don’t know if “overwhelmed” is the exact word every time, but I’m definitely… on alert. More than I think is normal.

Like, if I walk into a meeting room now, I don’t just walk in and sit down like I used to. I clock the exits first. I notice where the doors are, whether there’s another way out, who’s already in the room. And I’ll pick a chair where my back isn’t exposed—against a wall if I can manage it. I don’t like having someone behind me where I can’t see them.

Restaurants are the same way, which is embarrassing because it’s supposed to be just dinner. But I’ll scan the room before I’ve even looked at the menu. I watch people’s hands, especially if someone’s moving quickly or reaching into a bag or jacket. I know most of the time it’s nothing, but my body reacts before I can talk myself out of it.

It’s tiring, honestly. I try to make it look casual, like I just prefer a certain seat, but really I’m arranging myself so nobody can come up behind me and so I know how to get out if I need to.
Since that time, have you noticed that you often feel afraid, angry, or guilty — especially when you're reminded of what happened?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… I know I don’t feel good when I’m reminded of it, but if you’re asking whether I sit there thinking, “I’m afraid” or “I’m angry” or “I feel guilty,” it’s not always that obvious to me.

Sometimes it’s just this tight feeling, like I want to get away from the conversation or the place or whatever brought it up. And then afterward I might be irritated with myself because I think, why can’t I just handle this like a normal thing? But I don’t know that I’d call it guilt exactly. Or maybe I just don’t like using that word.

Anger… maybe in flashes, but I wouldn’t say I’m walking around angry all the time. And fear is hard too, because I don’t always feel scared in my head, if that makes sense. My body reacts before I’ve decided what I’m feeling.

So I guess the honest answer is: I’ve noticed reactions, yes, but I’m not sure I can neatly sort them into afraid, angry, or guilty.
Since that time, have you noticed that you’ve lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, or found it hard to feel positive emotions like happiness or love?

Yes… that’s actually one of the things I notice, even though I don’t always want to admit it.

I used to have things that could lift my whole mood, like salsa music. If I put it on in the kitchen, I’d start moving around without even thinking about it. It used to make the house feel alive, if that makes sense. Now I’ll put it on sometimes because I’m trying to make myself feel like I used to, and it’s like… I can hear it, I know I used to love it, but the good part doesn’t really land the same way.

Painting is like that too. I used to lose time doing it. I’d get caught up in the colors and the little details, and it felt peaceful. Now I’ll sit there with the supplies out, and I might even paint something, but it feels more like completing a task than enjoying it.

And Sunday dinner — that used to be a real thing for me. Cooking, planning what I was going to make, feeding people, having that warm feeling afterward. I still do it sometimes, or I try to, but I’m kind of going through the motions. I chop, stir, set the table, clean up… and I keep waiting for that feeling to show up, that comfort or happiness or love, and it just doesn’t come the way it used to. It’s not completely gone every second, but it feels muted. Like the volume got turned down on the good feelings.
